passage:
Day 9 since the college fest.
Sumit, 6:02 am: Good morning to the most beautiful mind I have ever met.
Parul, 7:40 am: Morning! Sorry, just woke up. Class at 9.
Sumit, 7:41 am: Skip it? I want to hear your voice.
Sumit, 7:45 am: You took long to reply. Did I say something wrong?
Parul, 7:46 am: No no, I was asleep.
Sumit, 7:46 am: I've never felt like this. It's like we were meant to find each other.
Parul, 7:50 am: It's only been nine days, haha. But honestly, nobody has ever talked to me like this.
Sumit, 7:51 am: Nine days, nine years, same thing when it's fate. Let's plan a trip together next month.
Parul, 7:53 am: A trip? I don't even know your middle name, or what you're like when you're grumpy.
Sumit, 7:53 am: You'll learn everything. Just don't pull away from me.
Parul typed "okay", deleted it, then typed it again.

qa.q: How many days had passed since the college fest?
qa.a: Nine days had passed since the college fest.

qa.q: What does Parul's line "nobody has ever talked to me like this" suggest about how Parul feels?
qa.a: Parul feels flattered and specially chosen by Sumit's attention, even while the joke about not knowing a middle name shows a small doubt about the speed.

qa.q: What could Parul do at the moment of typing "okay" about the trip?
qa.a: Parul could pause instead of agreeing, say a trip is too soon, keep going to class, and see whether Sumit stays kind when the pace slows.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit answered the middle-name joke with patience and ordinary details?
qa.a: Parul would get room to know a real person instead of a story about fate, and the pressure to reply fast and agree to a trip would ease.

grounding: A young adult, nine days after meeting someone, is flooded with early-morning messages and talk of fate and feels uniquely chosen, while the rush leaves no time to learn who Sumit really is.

passage:
The phone in Rukmini's lap buzzed again as the bus rattled past the sugarcane fields. Twelve messages from Tushar since breakfast. A photo of the temple fair where they had met eleven days ago, with a line: the day my life began. Another: No one will ever understand you like I do.
Rukmini pressed the phone to her chest. At home she was the quiet middle daughter, rarely asked what she thought. Tushar asked her everything.
"He wants me to meet his mother on Sunday," she told Minakshi, her bench-mate at the typing class.
Minakshi's eyebrows rose. "What does he do on weekdays?"
Rukmini opened her mouth and found she did not know. She knew his favourite song and that he called her his destiny, but not where he worked or who his friends were. She read the newest message twice, then left it unanswered until the bus stopped.

qa.q: How many messages had Tushar sent since breakfast?
qa.a: Tushar had sent twelve messages since breakfast.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini press the phone to her chest?
qa.a: She felt treasured and noticed; at home she was rarely asked what she thought, so Tushar's constant questions made her feel chosen.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do after realising she did not know what Tushar does on weekdays?
qa.a: She could hold off on meeting his mother on Sunday, ask plain questions about his work and friends, and give herself time to learn who he is.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see the rush from the outside?
qa.a: Minakshi seems puzzled that a family meeting is planned when basic facts are missing, and the raised eyebrows and simple question show gentle concern rather than judgement.

grounding: A young woman in a small town, swept up by messages about destiny from a man she met eleven days earlier, realises she knows little about his actual life.

passage:
"Sunaina, I can't sleep. I keep thinking about you."
"Mridul, it's two in the morning. We met on Saturday."
"And I've never felt like this. You're the one. I knew it the second I saw you at the fest."
Sunaina smiled into her pillow. Nobody had ever said anything like that to her.
"You don't even know me yet," she said, but softly.
"I know enough. It's destiny. My mother will love you."
"What does your mother do? Where did you grow up? I don't even know which college you're in."
"Does it matter? What matters is us."
"I guess…" She sat up. Forty messages since morning. Three voice notes. A poem. It felt wonderful. It also felt like being carried along by a river too fast to see the bank.
"Mridul, can we talk tomorrow? Properly. About normal things."
"Why? Don't you feel it too?"
She didn't answer right away.

qa.q: When did Sunaina and Mridul meet?
qa.a: We met on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel about Mridul's messages?
qa.a: Sunaina feels flattered and seen as never before, but also uneasy, like being carried along a river too fast to see the bank.

qa.q: What small step could help Sunaina here?
qa.a: She can slow things down, ask the ordinary questions she already raised, and take time to learn who Mridul really is before trusting the declarations.

qa.q: What does Mridul's reply "Does it matter?" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mridul wants to keep things on big feelings and destiny, avoiding the ordinary facts that would let Sunaina know him.

grounding: It shows a young adult swept up by constant messages and talk of destiny, feeling chosen while the speed hides who the person really is.

passage:
I'm Sarita, and I still think about those two weeks with Deepak.
We met at a friend's birthday. By the next morning, I had twenty messages. By day three, he was calling me "the one he'd been waiting for his whole life." By day seven, he'd sent flowers to my hostel and was talking about which city we'd live in.
I felt chosen. That's the only word. I'd always been the quiet one, the one people forgot to invite. And suddenly someone thought I was his destiny.
It was only when my roommate asked, "What's his surname? What does he actually do?" that I realised I didn't know. I knew he thought I was perfect. I didn't know if he was kind to waiters, or how he handled a bad day.
Everything had moved so fast that there had been no room to meet the real him.

qa.q: What did Deepak send by day seven?
qa.a: He'd sent flowers to Sarita's hostel.

qa.q: Why did Sarita feel so chosen?
qa.a: Sarita felt special and seen for the first time, because Sarita had always been the quiet one people forgot to invite.

qa.q: What question helped Sarita see what was missing?
qa.a: The roommate's question about his surname and job showed Sarita knew almost nothing real about him, which is a good reason to slow down.

qa.q: How might Sarita's roommate have seen those two weeks?
qa.a: The roommate probably felt concerned, noticing how fast it was moving and how little Sarita knew about Deepak.

grounding: A young adult recalls being flooded with messages and talk of destiny, feeling chosen while the speed left no room to know the person.

passage:
Hostel counsellor's note, girls' hostel, written by Sunaina, Wednesday.
Afreen came to see me today, glowing. She met a young man online nine days ago. She showed me her phone: good-morning messages every day, long voice notes, "you're my soulmate," "I've waited my whole life for you." He has asked her to meet his family next month.
She said, "Nobody has ever made me feel so special." I believe her. I could see how much it meant.
I asked gently what she knew about him apart from how he feels about her. She paused. She didn't know where he worked. She hadn't met him in person yet. She laughed, a bit uncertain.
I didn't tell her what to do. I told her that when something moves this fast, it's worth taking time to find out who he really is, and that meeting only in public places with friends told is sensible. She agreed to come back on Friday.

qa.q: How long ago did Afreen meet the young man online?
qa.a: She met him online nine days ago.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she came to the counsellor?
qa.a: Afreen felt glowing and special, saying nobody had ever made her feel that way, though she became uncertain when asked what she knew.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest without telling Afreen what to do?
qa.a: The counsellor suggested taking time to learn who he is, and meeting only in public with friends told, and asked her to come back on Friday.

qa.q: How might Afreen's view shift after the counsellor's question?
qa.a: Afreen may start to notice that she knows his feelings but not the person, which could make her slow down.

grounding: A counsellor records a young adult swept up by constant online declarations, feeling chosen while the speed leaves little room to know him.

passage:
12 March, 1:40 a.m.
Can't sleep. Sid sent good morning at 6, a voice note at lunch, a poem at 9, and he's still typing. Eight days since the library canteen and he says the universe planned it, that he's been waiting for me his whole life. Nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I feel seen, properly seen, for the first time ever.
Irawati asked tonight what Sid's family is like, what exactly he studies. I didn't know. I laughed it off, but it's sitting in my chest now. How can I feel like I know him completely when I couldn't answer two easy questions?
He wants to meet my parents next week. Part of me is floating. Part of me wants to say, can we just have coffee a few more times first?
I'm going to try that line tomorrow and see how he takes it.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How many days had passed since the library canteen?
qa.a: Eight days had passed since the library canteen.

qa.q: How is Jahnavi feeling about Sid's attention?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels thrilled and seen, almost floating, but also uneasy, because two easy questions about Sid had no answer.

qa.q: What small step could help Jahnavi now?
qa.a: Asking for a few more coffees before meeting parents slows the pace, and how Sid takes that gentle request will show a lot about him.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to see the romance?
qa.a: Irawati seems caring but curious, asking simple questions about Sid's family and studies that gently test how well Jahnavi really knows him.

grounding: Shows a young adult swept up by constant messages and talk of destiny, feeling seen yet unable to answer basic questions about the person.
